title: Two Keys
statement: A calculator display shows $1$. The calculator has exactly two keys: one adds $1$ to the displayed number, and the other multiplies the displayed number by $3$. How many different sequences of key presses change the display from $1$ to $30$?
hints: Think about the final key press of a sequence that ends on a number $n$. What could the display have shown just before that press?

Use recursion. Let $f(n)$ be the number of sequences taking the display from $1$ to $n$, then express $f(n)$ using the values of $f$ at the smaller numbers from which $n$ can be reached in one press. These are $n-1$ and, when $3$ divides $n$, also $\frac{n}{3}$.

With $f(n)$ as the number of sequences from $1$ to $n$, we have $f(1)=1$, and for $n \ge 2$ we have $f(n)=f(n-1)$ when $3$ does not divide $n$, and $f(n)=f(n-1)+f\left(\frac{n}{3}\right)$ when $3$ divides $n$. So $f$ changes only at multiples of $3$. Building the table gives $f(9)=5$ and $f(27)=23$, and just one more multiple of $3$ remains.
solution: Let $f(n)$ be the number of key sequences that take the display from $1$ to $n$. Both keys strictly increase the displayed positive number, so the display can never return to $1$. Hence only the empty sequence stays at $1$, and $f(1)=1$. Now take $n \ge 2$. Any sequence reaching $n$ has a last press, and we split into cases according to that press. If it is "add $1$", the earlier presses form a sequence from $1$ to $n-1$, and any such sequence can be extended in this way. If it is "multiply by $3$", then $3$ divides $n$ and the earlier presses form a sequence from $1$ to $\frac{n}{3}$, and again any such sequence can be extended. Sequences with different last presses are different, so no sequence is counted twice. Therefore $f(n)=f(n-1)$ when $3$ does not divide $n$, and $f(n)=f(n-1)+f\left(\frac{n}{3}\right)$ when $3$ divides $n$. So $f$ changes only at multiples of $3$, and at any other number it equals its value at the previous multiple of $3$, or $f(1)=1$ for $n=2$. For example, $f(2)=1$, $f(4)=f(5)=f(3)$ and $f(10)=f(9)$. Working through the multiples of $3$ gives $$f(3)=f(2)+f(1)=1+1=2,\quad f(6)=f(5)+f(2)=2+1=3,\quad f(9)=f(8)+f(3)=3+2=5,$$ $$f(12)=f(11)+f(4)=5+2=7,\quad f(15)=f(14)+f(5)=7+2=9,\quad f(18)=f(17)+f(6)=9+3=12,$$ $$f(21)=f(20)+f(7)=12+3=15,\quad f(24)=f(23)+f(8)=15+3=18,\quad f(27)=f(26)+f(9)=18+5=23,$$ $$f(30)=f(29)+f(10)=23+5=28.$$ The number of different sequences of key presses is $28$. Why this works. recursion, casework: splitting on the last key press writes each count in terms of counts for smaller numbers, which can be tabulated upwards from $1$.
